newsitem.title: USA: House committee approves term limits amendment.
newsitem.headline: House committee approves term limits amendment.

text.p: A House committee Tuesday approved a constitutional amendment to limit members of Congress to 12 years in office, but it is expected to fail in the full House next week.

The amendment would allow House members to serve no more than six two-year terms and would limit senators to two six-year terms. The measure needs a two-thirds majority in both chambers in order to go to the states for ratification.

"The American people want us to pass a term limits amendment. Seventy percent of them support it," Representative Bill McCollum, a Florida Republican, said before the House Judiciary Committee approved the amendment on a 19-12 vote.

McCollum said the amendment lacked the 290 votes needed for a two-thirds majority in the 435-member House. But he said he expected to get more than the 227 votes the measure got the last time it was voted on in 1995 when it was part of the 10-point Republican "Contract with America."
"The idea is to make progress," McCollum said.
The committee rejected a Democratic-backed amendment to apply term limits to current members upon ratification.

The Constitution sets two-year terms for House members and six years for senators, but puts no limits on how many terms they can serve. Presidents are limited to two four-year terms under a constitutional amendment ratified in 1951.

Several states voted in recent years to put term limits on their members of Congress, but the Supreme Court ruled that the only way to limit terms is through a constitutional amendment. Term limits supporters have gotten several states to pass laws to say on ballots if an incumbent member of Congress voted against term limits.
Supporters say term limits would make members of Congress more responsive to the public and take power away from career politicians who stay in office for 20 or 30 years.
Opponents say term limits would reduce choices for voters and force effective members to leave office, giving more power to unelected bureaucracts.

Representative John Conyers, a Michigan Democrat in his 17th term, said term limits were not needed because voters could replace members in any election. He said moe than half of the current Congress had been elected since 1990.
"The proponents of this legislation are playing politics with the Constitution. We already have term limits," he said.
